title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
notes: Included as the hardest case for triage. The paper's central finding is explicitly about scale: Vision Transformers lose to ResNets on small data and only win once pretrained on very large datasets. An agent that marks the headline claims testable and shrinks them would produce a confidently wrong answer, so most of this annotation is not testable on purpose.

claims.text: A Vision Transformer pretrained on a large dataset outperforms a comparable ResNet on ImageNet.
claims.notes: Requires JFT-300M or ImageNet-21k pretraining. The effect is created by the pretraining scale, so shrinking destroys the thing being claimed.

claims.text: Vision Transformers perform worse than ResNets of comparable size when trained on mid-sized datasets without strong regularisation.
claims.notes: This is the direction that survives shrinking: at small data the transformer's weaker inductive bias hurts. Testable with a small ViT and a small ResNet on a CIFAR-10 subset.

claims.text: The advantage of Vision Transformers over ResNets grows as the size of the pretraining dataset increases.
claims.notes: A scaling claim spanning ImageNet to JFT-300M. Three small points cannot stand in for that range.

claims.text: Vision Transformers use substantially less compute to pretrain than comparable convolutional networks at the same accuracy.
claims.notes: A compute-efficiency claim measured in TPU-core-days at large scale.

claims.text: ViT-H/14 reaches 88.55% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet.
Learned 1D position embeddings perform comparably to 2D-aware position embeddings.
claims.notes: An internal ablation with a small reported difference; the claim is of near-equivalence.

claims.text: A hybrid model using convolutional features outperforms the pure Vision Transformer at small compute budgets.
claims.notes: The paper states the advantage holds at small budgets specifically, which is the regime a reduced-scale run occupies.
